related_questions.question: How long does loss of taste last?

text_blocks.snippet: Loss of taste, or ageusia, can last anywhere from a few days to several weeks. For many, particularly with COVID-19, it's often a temporary condition, with most experiencing improvement within a month. However, some individuals may experience a permanent loss. The duration depends on the underlying cause.
snippet_highlighted_words: a few days to several weeks

list.title: COVID-19:
list.snippet: A significant percentage of people with COVID-19 experience loss of taste and smell, but most recover within a month. A study by the Mayo Clinic Health System found that about 90% of affected individuals see improvement within four weeks.

list.title: Other causes:
list.snippet: Loss of taste can also be caused by other factors like infections, head injuries, certain medications, or neurological conditions. The duration of these cases can vary widely, depending on the specific cause and severity.

list.title: Permanent loss:
list.snippet: While rare, some individuals may experience a permanent loss of taste due to factors like severe nerve damage.

related_questions.question: What to eat when taste buds are off?

text_blocks.snippet: When your taste buds are off, it's helpful to focus on foods that offer strong aromas, interesting textures, and appealing temperatures, as these can compensate for a diminished sense of taste. Experiment with different flavors and textures, and consider adding strong seasonings or acidic elements to stimulate your palate.
snippet_highlighted_words: foods that offer strong aromas, interesting textures, and appealing temperatures

list.title: Strong Aromas:
list.snippet: Foods with strong, appealing scents can help stimulate your senses. Consider foods like citrus fruits, garlic, onions, ginger, or herbs and spices like rosemary, thyme, or sage.

list.title: Variety of Textures:
list.snippet: Try crunchy foods like nuts, crackers, or toasted bread; creamy foods like yogurt or avocado; or chewy foods like dried fruit or jerky.

list.title: Temperature:
list.snippet: Experiment with hot, cold, or room temperature foods to see what feels most appealing.

list.title: Acidic Foods:
list.snippet: Citrus fruits (lemon, lime, orange), vinegar, or sour cream can help stimulate saliva production and potentially enhance flavor perception.

list.title: Seasonings and Spices:
list.snippet: Don't be afraid to experiment with different herbs, spices, and sauces to find what adds interest and excitement to your meals.

list.title: Salt:
list.snippet: If your doctor approves, you can try adding a little salt to your food, as it can enhance certain flavors, but be mindful of over-salting.

list.title: Small, Frequent Meals:
list.snippet: Eating smaller meals more often can be less overwhelming when you're not enjoying the taste of food.

list.title: Stay Hydrated:
list.snippet: Sufficient hydration is important for overall health and can help with dry mouth, which can affect taste.

list.title: Oral Hygiene:
list.snippet: Brushing your teeth and using mouthwash can help improve your sense of taste.
Citrus Fruits: Lemon, lime, and orange can be refreshing and help stimulate saliva.
Yogurt: A good source of protein and can be enjoyed on its own or with added flavors.
Smoothies and Shakes: Offer a variety of flavors and textures and can be easily customized.
Pickles: The sour and salty taste can be stimulating.
Foods with strong aromas: Garlic, onions, ginger, herbs, and spices.
High-protein foods and supplements: Important for maintaining nutrition when taste changes prevent you from eating normally, according to Stanford Health Care.
Foods with interesting textures: Crackers, nuts, dried fruit, and toasted bread.
Consult your doctor or a registered dietitian: If you are concerned about taste changes or if they persist, seek professional advice.

But other factors can contribute to loss of taste and smell, including: Nasal and sinus problems, such as allergies, sinusitis or nasal polyps. Viral infections, including the common cold and the flu.

text_blocks.snippet: Loss of taste is a recognized symptom of COVID-19, and it can be partial or complete. It's often accompanied by a loss of smell, and these sensory changes can persist in some individuals with Long COVID. While loss of taste can be caused by various factors, including aging, health problems, and medications, it's a common symptom associated with COVID-19, with some studies estimating that 60% of infected individuals experience it, according to Yale Medicine.
snippet_highlighted_words: Loss of taste is a recognized symptom of COVID-19, and it can be partial or complete

list.title: Prevalence:
list.snippet: Loss of taste (and smell) is a relatively common symptom of COVID-19.

list.title: Persistence:
list.snippet: In some cases, these sensory changes can persist long after the initial infection has resolved, leading to Long COVID.

list.title: Other Causes:
list.snippet: It's important to note that loss of taste can also be caused by other conditions, such as aging, certain health problems, medications, or even dental issues.

list.title: Distinguishing from other causes:
list.snippet: If you're experiencing loss of taste, it's a good idea to consult with a healthcare professional to determine the underlying cause, especially if you have other COVID-19 symptoms.
